I live in Silicon Valley, the home of AI and “innovation.” When I walk into my bank (like twice a year), at least three tellers and two banking assistants are there. I'm not sure what's happening with all the people here who only see ATMs, but our banks do much more than take deposits and withdraw cash. We have business and private loan officers, managers, and security. How do you not have this? How does your town do business? 🤔 When I go to the grocer, there's at least one checkout person (often three, depending on the time or day) and one person dealing with all the problems with the self-service kiosks. Our suburbs have even more staff. Don't get me started on Whole Foods (aka Whole Wallet). I've never seen so many staff members in a grocery store at all times of day. This is owned by one of the world's largest automaters, yet it has soooo many people working. How can your grocery stores only employ self-service kiosks? How is that possible? Who stocks the market and polices the customers? Who cleans the place? Our checkout people do all these things. Come to think of it, when I lived in a rural southern suburb, the Publix had even more checkout people. Target and Walmart had loads of checkout people that also ran stock, etc. This is all anecdotal, but it just shocks me how many comments here seem to imply their banks and grocery stores are fully automated, while finding that in the Bay Area, the heart of tech, seems nearly impossible to me. 🤷🏾‍♂️

AI will replace jobs when it makes financial sense. This is inevitable. Today, for example, big name actors in Hollywood are expensive and have often destroyed the profitability of the movies they star in. We see this practically every day, and it is causing unsustainable financial difficulties for financiers. In the coming decade, we can predict that many roles in blockbuster movies will be replaced by AI characters. It makes financial sense, and I would argue that it is inevitable. AI characters never age or die. They never do offscreen interviews. They will never have a contract dispute. They will never do something offscreen that causes a potential audience to not buy a ticket or turn to another channel. BUT, AI has made it easier and far less expensive for small teams of multitalented artists to create profitable movies. This technology gets better practically every day. The movie Flow, for example, demonstrates what is possible. It may have not been a blockbuster movie, but it proved that an entirely computer generated movie build by a handful of artists could turn a sizeable profit. Small, lightly funded teams can create more today than Hollywood could create a decade ago with a substantially higher budget and an army of artists. In less than a decade, a few people collaborating online will be able to make something that could compete with even the best blockbuster movies of today. Yes, those who refuse to adapt will lose their jobs. This is inevitable. But with this tech, more people will have the ability to create movies than ever before. If someone has a story to tell, they will not need to convince some production company to spend millions to put their story on the silver screen. They can get a few friends together and make that movie themselves. How awesome is that?
